claims.text: The baseline high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous microstructure without secondary high-conductivity phases.
The baseline alloy's lack of high-conductivity pathways causes comparatively low thermal conductivity.
Adding approximately 5 vol% Cu through powder mixing, HIP, and annealing will produce a uniform nanoscale dispersion of Cu precipitates.
The resulting Cu precipitates will be coherently embedded in the HEA matrix.
Copper precipitates have higher intrinsic thermal conductivity than the HEA matrix.
A uniform nanoscale Cu dispersion will provide conductive pathways through the HEA matrix.
The Cu precipitates will form continuous conductive pathways that lower thermal resistance.
Keeping the Cu precipitates nanoscale and coherently bonded will prevent large defects, harmful interfaces, and stress concentrations.
Approximately 5 vol% nanoscale Cu precipitates will improve effective thermal conductivity by at least about 10% relative to the baseline.
The Cu-modified alloy will retain yield strength comparable to that of the untreated HEA.
The Cu-modified alloy will retain ductility comparable to that of the untreated HEA.
The claimed thermal and mechanical benefits will persist near 700°C under representative cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
Excess Cu or inadequate precipitate control may cause phase instability.
Excess Cu or inadequate precipitate control may embrittle the alloy.
